title: NEMO
organization: Purdue Trace Labs / Humanoid Robotics Club
summary: NEMO is a small-scale humanoid research platform developed for biped locomotion and rapid mechanical iteration.
lede: A 20-DOF humanoid research platform developed for biped locomotion and rapid mechanical iteration.

cover.alt: Current NEMO humanoid robot on its test stand

heroMedia.alt: Current NEMO humanoid robot on its test stand

architecture.title: Hardware in the Loop
architecture.text: The lower body uses Unitree GO-M8010-6 actuators across three hip DOF, one knee DOF, and two ankle DOF per leg. We used a largely direct-drive architecture to limit gearing and mechanical complexity. Early block models established proportions, joint layout, mass distribution, and actuator demand; torque analysis then showed that several pitch joints required dual-motor configurations. Excessive width and center-of-mass placement in earlier concepts increased ankle torque, driving narrower layouts and major revisions to the hip, knee, and ankle architecture.

analysis.title: Stress & Structural Analysis
analysis.text: ANSYS FEA and hand calculations were used on key structural parts to identify where material could be removed while maintaining acceptable performance. Later revisions standardized parts, simplified motor housings, improved load paths, and moved appropriate non-load-bearing components from aluminum to printed polymers.

upperBody.title: Animatronic Design
upperBody.text: The upper body adds eight DOF across the shoulders, elbows, and neck. Its structure was developed around low mass, mechanical simplicity, and integration with the locomotion platform so the lower-body actuators were not unnecessarily overloaded.

testing.title: Sim-to-Real
testing.text: We designed and built an approximately six-foot-tall 80/20 test stand for safe locomotion work. Straps and a custom aluminum support arrangement provide fall protection while avoiding unnecessary restriction of the robot's motion. MuJoCo remained part of the development loop for gait stability, joint loading, and mechanical feasibility; the video shows the physical robot following locomotion commanded from simulation.

video.caption: Simulation-commanded locomotion on the physical test stand

locomotion.title: NEMO Shuffling
locomotion.text: We were able to finally move the project beyond CAD and simulation, and expose NEMO to the real world. Unfortunately, the motors we used for NEMO were not powerful enough for walking causing us to pivot to Ariel, a larger humanoid robot with more powerful actuators.

title: Zipline Projects
summary: Some of the work I did with my time at Zipline
lede: During my internship at Zipline, I worked across mechanical design, prototyping, test engineering, manufacturing, and hardware integration for UAV and ground-support systems. Below is some of the work I did with my time at Zipline

featured.title: Drone Transport Fixture
featured.summary: Designed and validated a rail-guided, ratcheting fixture for transferring a VTOL aircraft between ground level and a scissor lift, making the operation safer and possible with two operators.
featured.details: I developed the system in NX around a custom ratcheting mechanism, T-slot extrusion, and sheet-metal structure. First-principles strength and bending calculations informed component sizing, while 3D-printed parts, COTS hardware, quick-turn fabrication, and operator fit checks accelerated iteration and field validation.

media.alt: Completed transport fixture supporting an aircraft on a scissor lift
media.caption: Completed system during field operation

media.alt: Rail-guided drone transport fixture installed on a scissor lift
media.caption: Rail-guided fixture structure

featured.title: Portable UAV Data Offloader
featured.summary: Developed a portable, plug-and-play system for downloading aircraft logs in the field.
featured.details: I co-designed the custom PCBA and mechanical packaging around a compact computer, microcontroller, modular batteries, user interface, cooling, and supporting COTS hardware. The enclosure and mounting architecture prioritized field portability, DFM/DFA, and production of approximately 50 units, using MJF-printed components where appropriate.

media.caption: Portable enclosure and system packaging

featured.title: Structural Stability Testing
featured.summary: Deployed RTK GNSS instrumentation to monitor the positional and elevation stability of ground infrastructure over time.
featured.details: I developed a Python workflow to process measurements from multiple receivers and generate analysis and reports, with weather and rainfall data available as environmental context. The work centered on repeatable instrumentation, trend evaluation, and clear reporting.

media.caption: RTK instrumentation deployed for structural monitoring

additional.title: Electronics EOL Testing
additional.text: Built an end-of-line hardware test enclosure using machined, laser-cut, and 3D-printed components, integrating custom fixturing and electrical interfaces to validate PCBA, RF, and electromechanical subsystems. Integrated a Teensy-based RF test system with IIR filtering and configurable pass/fail thresholds.

title: Third Thumb
summary: I designed and prototyped a 3-DOF wearable robotic thumb with pin-jointed phalanges and servo-driven wire-tension actuation.
lede: A 3-DOF wearable robotic thumb exploring mechanical design, actuation, and human-device interaction.

heroMedia.alt: Third Thumb bench setup and actuation test

intro.title: A third thumb built around the hand.
intro.text: I designed and prototyped this 3-DOF Third Thumb after studying research from the University of Cambridge. Pin-jointed phalanges are actuated by a servo-driven wire-tensioning mechanism mounted across the hand and wrist. I iterated through multiple 3D-printed designs to improve flexion, extension, and grip stability.

media.alt: Assembled Third Thumb prototype on a hand

mechanism.title: Designed for motion, tolerance, and wearability.
mechanism.text: I studied hand anatomy—particularly how the muscles and bones work through the fingers—to inform the device geometry. Repeated iterations refined part tolerances and sizing so the rigid PLA assembly could move cleanly while fitting against my hand. A layer of Fosshape, a heat-activated soft thermoplastic, provided a flexible buffer between the device and my skin.

media.alt: CAD model of the articulated Third Thumb mechanism

integration.title: A wrist-mounted drive system.
integration.text: The actuator sits in a custom motor casing worn like a watch band. An Arduino Uno controls the servo-driven motion, bringing the tendon-style wire routing, wearable structure, and mechanical thumb together into one responsive prototype.

media.alt: Third Thumb prototype being worn and actuated

title: VTOL Aircraft
summary: I contributed to the construction and testing of a VTOL aircraft designed to transition between vertical and horizontal flight.
lede: Structural design, aerodynamic testing, and hardware validation for a transitioning VTOL aircraft.

intro.title: Built for the transition between lift and forward flight.
intro.text: I collaborated on the construction of a VTOL aircraft capable of transitioning from vertical to horizontal flight. My work covered structural design, aerodynamic testing, and hardware validation. I also helped assemble the V1 wings and empennage from carbon fiber, wood, and aluminum, reinforcing critical stress locations in the fuselage and empennage for transition loads.

media.alt: CAD rendering of the VTOL V2 aircraft design

mechanism.title: A V2 mount for fuselage comparisons.
mechanism.text: I designed the V2 fuselage prototype mount in SolidWorks for wind-tunnel testing of four fuselage prototypes. Using a dynamometer, we measured lift, drag, and pitching moment at multiple angles of attack. We determined airspeed from dynamic pressure, calculated dimensionless lift and drag coefficients, and compared lift-to-drag ratios across the models.

media.alt: VTOL fuselage prototype mounted for wind-tunnel testing

integration.title: A representative spar and thrust test rig.
integration.text: To measure motor thrust and carbon-fiber spar deflection under load, we designed and built a custom test rig. A 3D-printable wing cross-section let the spar mount in the same configuration used on the aircraft. A load cell was calibrated with known weights from 1 to 30 lb, producing a linear relationship used in the test software to convert load-cell output into thrust measurements.

title: H.A.R.R.Y.
summary: Our team developed H.A.R.R.Y., a mobile aluminum humanoid robot that demonstrated locomotion, chassis elevation, arm motion, gripping, and object transport.
lede: A mobile humanoid robot combining locomotion, vertical adjustment, and motor-pneumatic manipulation.

heroMedia.alt: Full assembled H.A.R.R.Y. mobile humanoid robot

intro.title: A mobile humanoid built around an aluminum chassis.
intro.text: Our team developed H.A.R.R.Y., a mobile aluminum humanoid robot designed to aid individuals with mobility challenges. Its 6-motor drivetrain chassis provided the stable platform needed to navigate different environments, while a rear motorized door securely held and transported objects. A four-motor linear-slide mechanism elevated the central chassis so the robot could interact with objects at different heights.

media.alt: H.A.R.R.Y. aluminum chassis and vertical lift structure

mechanism.title: Motorized shoulders with pneumatic elbow motion.
mechanism.text: We designed the arms around a motorized shoulder mechanism and pneumatic circuits. The shoulder provided a broad range of motion, while the pneumatically actuated elbow handled contraction and extension. Adding a flow regulator reduced aggressive elbow contractions and made the movement smoother and more controlled.

media.alt: H.A.R.R.Y. shoulder and arm assembly

integration.title: Designed to grip, lift, and demonstrate the full system.
integration.text: Together, the drivetrain, lift, and arm systems allowed the prototype to elevate its chassis, perform complex arm movements, and grip and lift objects weighing up to 50 N. Our team presented the working robot and its findings to industry professionals.

media.alt: H.A.R.R.Y. arm prototype and pneumatic mechanism

title: Competition Robot
summary: As team captain, I co-developed a VEX Spin Up robot integrating disk intake, flywheel shooting, pneumatic indexers, and expansion systems.
lede: VEX Spin Up competition robot integrating disk intake, flywheel shooting, pneumatics, and expansion systems.

heroMedia.alt: Full VEX Spin Up competition robot

intro.title: A coordinated system for intake, shooting, and expansion.
intro.text: As team captain, I co-developed our VEX Spin Up competition robot around a vertical intake for rapid disk collection, two pneumatic piston indexers, and a 3600 RPM flywheel for shooting disks into raised baskets. We also built a pneumatic expansion mechanism that released a tensioned string across the field, plus a pneumatic- and rubber-band-tensioned mesh blocker for defense. The team won the NJ TSA Championships and qualified for VEX Nationals and the VEX World Championships.
